extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in philosophy, skepticism, and Montaigne-style moral essays
extracted.subtask_description: An expository moral-philosophical essay discussing Pyrrhonism, dogmatism, the uses of inquiry and belief, and the practical relation between truth, utility, and religion. The page surveys ancient opinions and evaluates styles of philosophizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of judgment (Pyrrhonism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure, entire, perfect, and absolute suspension of judgment: to assert nothing and hold no fixed assent; to make use of reason to inquire and debate but not to fix and determine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as conceiving a perpetual confession of ignorance and a judgment without bias or inclination. Examples and paraphrase: 'I assert nothing; it is no more so than so... Nothing seems true, that may not seem false.' Authors represent this variously and obscurely; Pyrrhonism seeks to suspend assent when appearances are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reason to inquire, not to determine
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason's role is to inquire and debate rather than to establish absolute certainty or fixed dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts inquiry with determinative speaking: 'They make use of their reason to inquire and debate, but not to fix and determine.' This is illustrated by philosophers who compile probable arguments rather than asserting final truths (e.g., Timæus/Plato quoted: speak as a man to a man; give probable conjectures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical action governed by probabilities and appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary life one should act on probable circumstances, appearances, and conveniences (e.g., vessel tightness, experience of the pilot, season), even while suspending philosophical assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pyrrhonian practice: when going to sea follow probable indicators and then be governed by appearances provided no manifest contradiction. The practical arts often proceed by conjecture rather than certain knowledge; one may live with liberty and convenience without fixed assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearing prejudice for tranquility and repose
rubrics_metrics.description: A soul free from prejudice gains tranquillity and repose; freedom from premature assent is valuable for peace of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes 'A soul clear from prejudice has a marvellous advance towards tranquillity and repose.' This is offered as a benefit of skeptical suspension of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of humility, docility, and religious/civil obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple, incurious minds that yield to laws, religion, and custom are more docile and easier to govern and more apt to receive faith; humility and willingness to be guided are praised for social utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts incurious minds with over-vigilant wits, arguing the former are more receptive to divine knowledge and social order. Examples include Ecclesiastes citations and the practical benefits of yielding to established practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dogmatic tone often rhetorical, not evidentiary
rubrics_metrics.description: Many dogmatists adopt a confident, assured manner not because they can establish certainty, but to produce effect or show how far their search has proceeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation and paraphrase: 'Which the learned rather feign than know.' Cicero/Plato examples; authors may speak with assurance 'that what I say is fixed and certain' though they present probabilities. Guidance: be skeptical of apparent certainties as rhetorical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility may legitimately trump abstract truth in presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some philosophical or legislative fictions are justified when they serve useful social ends; it is often necessary for the benefit of men 'to deceive them' or to employ profitable untruths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's noble lie and the Laws are invoked: when legislating or instructing the vulgar, presenting fiction that produces advantageous effects is defensible. Example: limit public song to poetry that tends to useful ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deliberate obscurity and bombast as vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty, abstruseness, bombast, and riddling phrase are often devices of the learned to conceal vanity; such obscurity pleases fools but is a poor defense of true understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne observes learned men use difficulty 'like jugglers' and quotes: 'Bombast and riddle best do puppies please.' Anti-pattern: obscurity used to impress rather than to clarify; critics (Cicero, Epicurus) avoided quoting to prevent misleading the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning should profit teachers towards virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning that brings no virtue to its teachers is of little value; practical, moral benefit is a primary test of valuable learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne quotes Socrates: he esteems most that which profits teachers themselves to virtue. 'Parum mihi placeant eæ littero quo ad virtutem doctoribus nihil profuerunt.' Education is subordinate to moral improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some speculative writings are mere intellectual exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ancient and learned men produced conjectures and varied opinions not because they believed them as foundation truths but to exercise their wits in difficult matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'They seem not so much themselves to have believed what they said, as to have had a mind to exercise their wits in the difficulty of the matter.' This explains inconstancy and diversity of opinions among admirable men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious images, ceremonies, and sensory devotion have practical benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensory elements (crucifixes, pictures, ceremonies, music) in religion 'warm the souls of the people' and produce advantageous effects even if they are not literally true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne defends use of tangible signs and rites as necessary aids for human belief: 'It is man that believes and prays.' Social/pastoral utility is emphasized over doctrinal purity in public practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theology should acknowledge divine incomprehensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: It is more reasonable to acknowledge God as an incomprehensible first cause than to imagine Him in humanlike, limited forms; attributing human passions to divinity is a weakness of understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises opinions that render God indefinite and without limitation; he criticizes attributing desires, anger, marriages, fevers, etc., to gods. Anti-pattern: anthropomorphizing the divine diminishes transcendence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promises of the afterlife should be conceived as truly other, not earthly analogues
rubrics_metrics.description: If heavenly rewards are merely enlarged versions of earthly sensual pleasures, they cannot be truly infinite or divine; divine beatitude must be unimaginable and of another order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues Plato's and other sensual depictions of the afterlife (tapestried paradises, wenches, etc.) are accommodations to mortal appetites and thus inadequate as conceptions of the divine. 'Eye hath not seen...the things that God hath prepared.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity and contradiction of philosophical opinions counsel humility
rubrics_metrics.description: The wide variety and contradiction among philosophical positions shows human reason's variability and limits, and invites humility rather than certitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts numerous differing ancient theories about gods and the world (Thales, Anaximander, Plato, Aristotle, etc.) to show the instability of human doctrines. Guidance: interpret diversity as instructive and humbling.
